en: Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery, together with a great saṅgha of monks, numbering twelve hundred and fifty monks.
There, the Blessed One addressed the monks.

"Monks, these five benefits should be understood to arise from the offering of a mandala. What are the five? Namely: one's own mind becomes serene; the minds of others become serene; the deities become joyful; one becomes pleasing to behold and performs and accumulates karma conducive to being pleasing to behold; and after the breaking up of the body, one is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world, among the gods.
Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further said this:
The great-souled one attains clarity of mind and likewise gladdens the minds of others;
he becomes serene through his meritorious deeds, and the gods become thrilled and joyful.
No diseases shall afflict the body of him who, for the sake of the Buddha, constructs a maṇḍala. [1]

And no diseases arise in his body; cow dung mixed with water is his gift, sweeping is his ethical discipline, the removal of tiny ants is his patience, and the act of rising to perform work is his vigor.
Meditation is the one-pointedness of mind at that very moment, and wisdom is its brilliant, well-drawn lines;
by constructing the maṇḍala of the Sage, one obtains these six perfections.
One becomes golden-hued and liberated from all diseases.

Having performed these physical deeds in this excellent home of the Sugata, one is born in a royal lineage, enriched with wealth and gold, distinguished among gods and men, and possessing a radiant splendor like the moon. [3]
The Blessed One spoke thus, and with joyful minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
The tenth sūtra, the Maṇḍalakānuśaṃsāsūtra, is completed.
